fetched_contents.text: Primogeniture in: Elgar Encyclopedia of Family Business Primogeniture refers to the preference in inheriting the business given to the male firstborn child. Primogeniture exempts the incumbent to make a choice among several potential successors and strengthens certain features of the family socioemotional wealth invested in the firm. In addition, the rule of primogeniture may also prevent the fragmentation of ownership across generations, which could create issues in decision making and commitment to the firm by different family branches. However, the application of the male preference primogeniture rule has major drawbacks, the most relevant ones being: (i) the implicit exclusion of daughters from the succession and (ii) the lower importance of competence-based successors’ assessment. The primogeniture principle is increasingly challenged by the evolution in society. In particular, the awareness of daughters’ issues in succession has substantially grown in the recent decades, along with the change in professional and family roles of women in society.

Our work reveals that things are much more complex and diverse than research tells us in terms of daughters, their families, and their businesses. Daughters are not only “in” or “out” of the family business. They can be included in a variety of ways, at different moments, following different paths, in a diversity of contexts. Based on 10 years of qualitative research data on family business succession, we explain and discuss how gender dynamics in the family and the business systems affect succession practices and outcomes, beyond the individual level analysis. We used six selected and contrasted cases to illustrate the influence that gender, birth order, family inherited culture, business hierarchies and history, interpersonal relationships (parents-heirs-other stakeholders), as well as ownership transfers, governance rules and management procedures have on intergenerational succession, and particularly in daughters’ family business inclusion. Primogeniture creates direct barriers to daughters' succession and authority by privileging male firstborn heirs and reducing daughters' access to core family business roles. The evidence shows that primogeniture is defined as the preference in inheriting the business given to the male firstborn child, which implicitly excludes daughters from succession and lowers the importance of competence-based assessment of successors [N1-F1]. This mechanism is not merely symbolic; it shapes who is treated as a legitimate successor and who is not. In family business contexts, daughters are often excluded as candidates for succession, and studies show that gender-related factors greatly affect succession decisions [N2-R4][N6-R4]. This means that daughters are typically denied or delayed in roles and decision-making powers that are central to ownership, leadership, and control.

The evidence also indicates that daughters are frequently excluded from ownership, management, or symbolic leadership. One source states that succession is “very much biased by gender” and that daughters are “almost always excluded as candidates” [N2-R4][N6-R4]. Another source notes that primogeniture may prevent fragmentation of ownership across generations, which can create issues in decision making and commitment to the firm by different family branches [N1-F1]. This suggests that daughters are often not positioned to control the business or shape its direction, even when they are part of the family. Instead, primogeniture can force daughters into peripheral or symbolic roles. The same source says that primogeniture “exempts the incumbent to make a choice among several potential successors” and that the rule strengthens family socioemotional wealth invested in the firm [N1-F1]. This framing implies that daughters may be assigned symbolic or supporting roles rather than leadership roles, even if they are present in the family.

The evidence also supports the idea that daughters are not simply excluded from leadership but are often delayed or deprioritized. For example, one study notes that daughters may feel inhibited or face barriers to leadership because of gender issues in the succession process [N2-R2]. Another source indicates that parental instrumental support and family business work experience positively influence daughters’ succession intentions, which implies that daughters must overcome entrenched barriers to even consider succession [N2-R1]. Taken together, these sources show that primogeniture acts as a structural barrier by denying daughters direct access to ownership, management, and symbolic leadership, while also pushing them into less central roles or delaying their entry into leadership altogether [N1-F1][N2-R4][N6-R4].

Primogeniture creates direct barriers to daughters' succession and authority by privileging male firstborn heirs and reducing daughters' access to core family business roles. The evidence shows that primogeniture is defined as the preference in inheriting the business given to the male firstborn child, which implicitly excludes daughters from succession and lowers the importance of competence-based assessment of successors [N1-F1]. This mechanism is not merely symbolic; it shapes who is treated as a legitimate successor and who is not. In family business contexts, daughters are often excluded as candidates for succession, and studies show that gender-related factors greatly affect succession decisions [N2-R4][N6-R4]. This means that daughters are typically denied or delayed in roles and decision-making powers that are central to ownership, leadership, and control.

The evidence also indicates that daughters are frequently excluded from ownership, management, or symbolic leadership. One source states that succession is “very much biased by gender” and that daughters are “almost always excluded as candidates” [N2-R4][N6-R4]. Another source notes that primogeniture may prevent fragmentation of ownership across generations, which can create issues in decision making and commitment to the firm by different family branches [N1-F1]. This suggests that daughters are often not positioned to control the business or shape its direction, even when they are part of the family. Instead, primogeniture can force daughters into peripheral or symbolic roles. The same source says that primogeniture “exempts the incumbent to make a choice among several potential successors” and that the rule strengthens family socioemotional wealth invested in the firm [N1-F1]. This framing implies that daughters may be assigned symbolic or supporting roles rather than leadership roles, even if they are present in the family.

The evidence also supports the idea that daughters are not simply excluded from leadership but are often delayed or deprioritized. For example, one study notes that daughters may feel inhibited or face barriers to leadership because of gender issues in the succession process [N2-R2]. Another source indicates that parental instrumental support and family business work experience positively influence daughters’ succession intentions, which implies that daughters must overcome entrenched barriers to even consider succession [N2-R1]. Taken together, these sources show that primogeniture acts as a structural barrier by denying daughters direct access to ownership, management, and symbolic leadership, while also pushing them into less central roles or delaying their entry into leadership altogether [N1-F1][N2-R4][N6-R4].

Legal and institutional structures amplify primogeniture’s barriers by reinforcing male-preference inheritance and by shaping family governance in ways that limit daughters’ control. The evidence shows that primogeniture is not only a customary practice but also a rule that may be embedded in family socioemotional wealth and ownership structures [N1-F1]. This means that legal norms and family governance can interact with primogeniture to exclude daughters. One source notes that primogeniture may prevent fragmentation of ownership across generations, which can create issues in decision making and commitment by different family branches [N1-F1]. That same logic can also limit daughters’ control because the preference for male heirs can concentrate authority in fewer hands, reducing the likelihood that daughters will inherit the firm or participate in major decisions.

Inheritance laws and corporate ownership rules are central to this dynamic. The evidence indicates that primogeniture is the right of the firstborn legitimate child to inherit the family estate, in preference to siblings [N1-R3][N1-R4]. This legal framing supports male-first succession and makes daughters’ exclusion more institutionalized. The source also states that primogeniture may prevent fragmentation of ownership across generations, which implies that inheritance rules can be designed to preserve a single line of control rather than allowing daughters to inherit alongside or independently of male heirs [N1-F1]. At the same time, family business succession planning is described as a complex process involving estate planning, ownership transfer, and governance rules [N5-R2][N5-R3]. This suggests that institutional arrangements—such as family governance structures, ownership transfers, and succession planning—can reinforce primogeniture by privileging one heir over others.

Institutional biases in family business governance also reinforce exclusion. The evidence shows that family business succession is influenced by interpersonal relationships, family reputation, and other social pressures [N2-R2][N3-R2][N6-R3]. These pressures can be embedded in governance structures, such as how succession is discussed, who is considered a “candidate,” and how leadership roles are allocated. The source on daughters’ inclusion notes that gender dynamics in the family and business systems affect succession practices and outcomes, beyond individual-level analysis, and that ownership transfers, governance rules, and management procedures matter [N4-F2]. This indicates that governance structures are not neutral; they can codify or reinforce male-preference primogeniture. Overall, legal and institutional structures amplify primogeniture’s barriers by privileging male heirs, concentrating ownership, and embedding exclusion in family governance and succession planning [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4][N5-R2][N5-R3].

This suggests that in some contexts, daughters can still enter succession, but only under very specific conditions, while in other contexts, they are excluded by default [N4-R1]. The cross-cultural source also states that daughters’ inclusion in family business succession can take place in a variety of ways, at different moments, following different paths, in diverse contexts [N4-F2]. National legal systems shape succession outcomes in several ways. ### 4) Cross-cultural variation in daughter succession under primogeniture

Primogeniture acts as a cultural barrier to daughters in family businesses because it is embedded in gendered expectations, family identity, and institutional practices that prioritize male heirs.
